title: Containers (Basic): Container Registry, Container Instances and Container Apps
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain how a container differs from a virtual machine and why an image makes a deployment repeatable.
- Describe images, tags, digests and registries, and choose an Azure Container Registry tier and sign-in method.
- Explain how Azure Container Apps uses environments, revisions, ingress and scale rules, including scale to zero.
- Choose between Azure Container Instances, Azure Container Apps, Azure Kubernetes Service and App Service for a given container workload.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Dewi has rewritten the storefront's product pages, and on her laptop they fly. On the test server they crash: the server has an older Python runtime and is missing an image library. "It works on my machine" has become the most expensive sentence in the office. Pak Budi spends his evenings matching library versions by hand, and Rizky, the contractor, wants to "just put everything in Kubernetes".

Ibu Sari has a different worry. During the Harbolnas 12.12 sale, traffic jumps tenfold for a few hours; at three in the morning on a normal Tuesday almost nobody shops. She does not want to pay for sale-sized servers all year. There is also a nightly job that imports supplier prices for ten minutes and then sits idle for the rest of the day.

Today you answer two questions. How do we package the storefront once so that it runs the same everywhere? And which Azure service should run that package, so that we pay for shoppers rather than for idle servers?

Reading

1. Containers in one picture

A container is a running process that carries its own application code, runtime and libraries, kept apart from every other process on the same machine. Unlike a virtual machine, a container does not bring its own operating system kernel. All containers on a host share the host's kernel, and the kernel itself fences them off: each container sees only its own files and processes and may use only the CPU and memory it was given.

That one design choice explains almost every difference you will meet. A VM boots a whole operating system, so it takes minutes to start and its disk image is measured in gigabytes. A container starts a process, so it is ready in seconds, and its package is often tens or hundreds of megabytes. Many more containers than VMs fit on the same hardware, which is why cloud providers can rent you containers by the second.

The package you ship is a container image: a read-only, layered file system plus a little metadata, such as the command to run and the default environment variables. You describe how to build it in a text file called a Dockerfile. Each instruction adds a layer, and layers are cached and shared, so a code change usually rebuilds and uploads only the thin top layer, not the runtime underneath.

FROM python:3.12-slim                  # base layer: OS libraries and the Python runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt    # dependency layer, rebuilt only when requirements change
COPY . .                               # your code: the layer that changes most often
EXPOSE 8080                            # documents the port; it does not open anything by itself
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:app"]

A handy way to remember the difference: the image is a sealed meal kit with every ingredient measured; a container is that kit cooked and served. Cook the same kit in a hundred kitchens and you get the same dish, which is exactly what Dewi needs. Her laptop, the test environment and production all run the same image, so "works on my machine" turns into "works in the image".

| Virtual machine (Lunch 06) | Container
What is virtualized | The hardware; every VM runs its own OS kernel | The operating system; containers share the host kernel
Typical start time | Minutes | Seconds
Typical package size | Gigabytes | Megabytes to a few hundred megabytes
How you update | Patch the running guest OS and app in place | Build a new image and replace the container
Where state lives | Often on the VM's disks | Outside the container: a database, storage or a mounted volume
Good for | Lift-and-shift, full OS control, legacy software | APIs, web front ends, microservices, short jobs

Two habits follow. First, treat containers as disposable: never "fix" a running container by hand, because the next replacement will not have your fix. Change the image instead. Second, keep data outside the container, in Azure SQL, Azure Cosmos DB or Azure Storage (Lunches 07, 11 and 12), so that losing a container never loses an order.

2. Images, tags and Azure Container Registry

A registry stores and serves images. Inside it, a repository holds the versions of one image (for example storefront), and each version carries one or more tags such as v1 or 2026.10.23. Every image also has a digest, a SHA-256 hash of its content. A tag is a movable label; a digest never changes. A full image reference reads like an address: acrnusa12345.azurecr.io/storefront:v1 means login server, repository and tag.

Public registries hold images that anyone can pull: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry and Microsoft Artifact Registry (mcr.microsoft.com), where Microsoft publishes its own images, including the sample web app you will use in the lab. Your own images belong in a private registry. Azure Container Registry (ACR) is Azure's managed private registry: it lives in your subscription and your region, close to the services that pull from it, and it stores container images, Helm charts and other OCI artifacts behind Microsoft Entra ID sign-in.

Tier | Included storage | What stands out | Use it when
Basic | 10 GiB | Same APIs and Entra ID sign-in as the other tiers; lowest throughput | Learning, labs, small teams
Standard | 100 GiB | More storage and throughput, anonymous pull, artifact cache rules | Most production workloads
Premium | 500 GiB | Geo-replication, private endpoints, customer-managed keys, network rules, connected registries | Several regions, private networks, regulated data

All three tiers are zone redundant by default in regions with availability zones, and you can change tier later without downtime (moving down from Premium means removing Premium-only features first). Storage beyond the included amount is charged per GiB, so delete old tags you no longer need.

There are three ways to get an image into ACR:

- Push an image you built locally with Docker: az acr login, then docker push.
- Import an image from another registry with az acr import. The copy happens inside Azure, so you need no Docker at all. This is what the lab does.
- Build in the cloud with ACR Tasks: az acr build uploads your source folder and builds the image in Azure. Tasks can also rebuild automatically when you commit to Git or when a base image gets a security patch.

Important: At the time of writing (October 2026), ACR Tasks runs are paused for subscriptions that use Azure free credits; a build fails with TasksOperationsNotAllowed. That is why the lab imports a public image and keeps the cloud build as an optional extra. Check the ACR Tasks documentation for the current status.

Who may pull? People sign in with Entra ID (az acr login). Azure services should use a managed identity that holds the AcrPull role on the registry, so no password exists anywhere. ACR also has an admin user, a single shared username and password; it is off by default and should stay off outside quick experiments. A newer role-assignment mode, "RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions", lets you scope access to individual repositories. Microsoft says it will become the default; in that mode the legacy AcrPull role is ignored and you assign Container Registry Repository Reader instead.

A word about the latest tag: it is only a default name, not a promise that the image is the newest. Deploy explicit tags such as v1 or a date, so you always know what is running and can roll back to the previous tag in seconds.

3. Azure Container Instances: one container, right now

Azure Container Instances (ACI) is the shortest path from an image to a running container. You name the image, the CPU cores and memory, the ports and, optionally, a DNS name label. Seconds later the container answers at label.region.azurecontainer.io. You never see a VM or a cluster, and you pay per second for the CPU and memory allocated while it runs.

The unit you deploy is a container group: one or more containers on the same host that share a network, storage volumes and a lifecycle, much like a pod in Kubernetes. Multi-container groups are available for Linux containers; a typical pair is an app plus a small log-shipping helper. Each group is isolated at the hypervisor level, so a neighbour on the same hardware cannot see into it.

A restart policy tells ACI what to do when the process ends. Always, the default, suits web servers. OnFailure retries only after errors. Never suits run-to-completion work, such as Nusantara Retail's nightly price import: the job runs for ten minutes, exits, and the meter stops.

Day-to-day operations stay small too. az container logs shows what the process printed, az container attach streams that output live, and az container exec opens a shell inside a running container when you need to look around. You pass settings as environment variables, mark sensitive ones as secure so they are hidden from the resource's properties, and mount an Azure Files share when the container needs files that outlive it. Two limits catch people out: ACI runs x64 (AMD64) images only, so an image built only for ARM on a laptop will not start, and a very large image slows every start because it must be pulled first.

ACI is deliberately simple, and that simplicity is also its limit. It does not autoscale, it does not load-balance across copies, and it has no revisions or managed certificates; to run five copies you create five container groups. A group's public IP address can change after a restart, so always use the DNS name. To pull from a private ACR, ACI needs a user-assigned managed identity with AcrPull; it cannot use a system-assigned identity for image pulls.

Newer options build on the same engine: Spot containers run interruptible work at a discount, confidential containers protect data while it is in memory, NGroups keep a set of related container groups running with rolling upgrades across zones, and virtual nodes let an AKS cluster burst pods into ACI. For Nusantara Retail, ACI fits the price import, a quick test of a vendor's image, or a short-lived build agent.

4. Azure Container Apps: serverless apps that scale to zero

Azure Container Apps runs web apps, APIs, background workers and jobs from container images on a serverless platform. Under the hood it uses Kubernetes and open-source projects (KEDA for event-driven scaling, Envoy for ingress and Dapr for microservice building blocks), but it never asks you to manage, upgrade or even see the Kubernetes API.

Four building blocks matter:

- An environment is a secure boundary around a group of apps. Apps in one environment share a virtual network and a Log Analytics workspace and can call each other by name. The default type is a workload profiles environment, which offers the serverless Consumption profile plus optional Dedicated profiles with reserved hardware.
- A container app is your application. Its configuration (ingress, secrets, registry sign-in, revision mode) applies to the whole app.
- A revision is an immutable snapshot of the app's template: image, environment variables, CPU and memory, and scale rules. Changing anything in the template creates a new revision; changing ingress, secrets or the traffic split does not.
- A replica is one running copy of a revision. Replicas come and go as load changes.

Ingress publishes the app. External ingress gives it a public HTTPS address on azurecontainerapps.io, with the certificate handled for you; internal ingress keeps it reachable only inside the environment or your virtual network. You also declare the target port: the port your process listens on inside the container.

Warning: The most common first-deployment mistake is a wrong target port. If the image listens on 80 and you set 8080, the platform cannot reach your app: the revision never becomes healthy and every request fails. EXPOSE in a Dockerfile is documentation only, so check the image's documentation and set the target port to match.

Each revision scales between a minimum and a maximum number of replicas, by default 0 and 10 (at the time of writing you can configure up to 1,000). Scale rules decide when to add replicas: an HTTP rule watches concurrent requests per replica (10 by default), a TCP rule watches connections, and a custom rule can use any KEDA scaler, such as Service Bus queue length. The arithmetic is simple: 45 concurrent requests with a target of 10 gives ceil(45 ÷ 10) = 5 replicas, capped at your maximum.

With a minimum of zero, a quiet app scales to zero after a cool-down (300 seconds by default) and costs nothing for compute while it sleeps. The trade-off is a cold start: the first request after a quiet spell waits a few seconds while a replica starts. Production apps that must answer instantly set a minimum of one or two; replicas that sit idle at that minimum are billed at a reduced idle rate.

The revision mode controls releases. In single mode (the default) a new revision takes over once it is ready, which gives zero-downtime updates. In multiple mode several revisions stay active and you split traffic by percentage, for example 80% on the proven v1 and 20% on the new v2 (a canary release), then move to 100% when you are confident. A labels mode, in preview at the time of writing, adds named labels such as staging.

Two more features are worth knowing by name. Dapr is an optional sidecar that gives your code standard APIs for service-to-service calls, publish and subscribe messaging and state, so the code is not tied to one message broker. Jobs run containers to completion on demand, on a schedule or when events arrive, which makes them a second option for the nightly price import.

On the Consumption plan you pay per second for the vCPU and memory your replicas use, plus a small charge per million requests. Each subscription gets a monthly free grant (at the time of writing, 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests), which is why the lab costs next to nothing.

5. Choosing where your container runs

The same image can run on four different Azure services. The difference is how much platform you get, and how much platform you have to look after.

| Container Instances | Container Apps | Azure Kubernetes Service | App Service (Web App for Containers)
Mental model | One container group, on demand | Serverless apps and jobs | Your own managed Kubernetes cluster | Managed web hosting that runs your image
You look after | Each container group | Apps, revisions and scale rules | Nodes, upgrades, add-ons and Kubernetes objects (less with AKS Automatic) | The App Service plan and app settings
Scaling | None built in; create more groups | Automatic by HTTP, TCP or events, down to zero | Pod and node autoscalers you configure | Manual or autoscale of the plan; no scale to zero
You pay for | Per second of vCPU and memory | Per second of use plus requests (free grant), or Dedicated profiles | The node VMs, plus a fee on the Standard and Premium tiers | Plan instances, whether busy or idle
Kubernetes API | No | No | Yes | No
Best for | Jobs, quick tests, build agents, burst capacity | Microservices, APIs, event-driven workers, apps that idle | Platform teams, Helm charts and operators, fine-grained control | Classic web apps that want deployment slots and built-in sign-in

Read the table from left to right as "more control, more responsibility". Start with the simplest service that meets the requirement. For most of Nusantara Retail's new container workloads, that is Container Apps.

Move to AKS (Lunch 29) when you need the Kubernetes API itself: a vendor ships its software as a Helm chart with custom operators, you need agents on every node (DaemonSets), you want precise control over node hardware or a service mesh, or a platform team will run many applications for many teams on one shared cluster. Choose App Service (Lunch 10) when the app is a classic website and you value deployment slots, built-in authentication and custom domains more than container-level control; the container is then simply your packaging format. Event-driven functions can also run in containers, which Lunch 14 covers.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Here is the plan you take back to Ibu Sari:

- One registry. An ACR named acrnusa… holds every image. The labs use Basic; production starts on Standard and moves to Premium only if the team needs private endpoints or a second region. Images get explicit version tags, services pull with managed identities, and the admin user stays off.
- The storefront on Container Apps. External ingress on the right target port, an HTTP scale rule and a maximum sized for the 12.12 sale. The test environment keeps a minimum of zero to save money; production keeps a minimum of one or two, accepting a small idle charge so that the first shopper of the morning never waits.
- Safer releases. Multiple revision mode lets Dewi send 20% of shoppers to a new version, watch the error rate, and then move to 100%, or back to 0% in seconds.
- The nightly price import. A scheduled Container Apps job, or ACI with the Never restart policy. Either way it bills for ten minutes, not twenty-four hours.
- Data stays outside. Orders stay in Azure SQL and the catalogue in Cosmos DB; secrets move to Key Vault in Lunch 15. Containers can be replaced at any moment without losing anything.

Data residency still applies. Production would run in Indonesia Central (Jakarta), while the labs use Southeast Asia for the broadest service availability. Before you commit, check that each service and feature you need is offered in your chosen region.

Pause and think: the storefront app has a minimum of zero replicas. At 07:00 a push notification brings 2,000 shoppers in one minute. What happens to the first few requests, which single setting would you change for production, and what does that change cost?

Going deeper: Lunch 29 · Containers (Advanced): Azure Kubernetes Service (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/29-containers-advanced-aks.html) takes the same images onto a full Kubernetes cluster.

Field notes from Stefanus

Fix the recipe, not the dish. My rule for containers is simple: whatever I learn by opening a shell inside a running container goes back into the Dockerfile the same day. The shell is for looking around, never for repairs, because the next replica starts from the image and forgets every manual change. In design reviews I ask one question about each container: what do we lose if it disappears right now? Any answer other than "nothing" means something lives in the wrong place, such as uploaded photos in a local folder, shopping carts held in memory or logs that never leave the container. And I read the Dockerfile as carefully as the code: a password copied into an early layer stays readable to anyone who can pull the image, even if a later instruction deletes the file.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Comparing Container Apps with other Azure container options (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/compare-options) — Microsoft's own guidance on when to pick each service.
- Microsoft Learn: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/scale-app) — every rule type, the defaults and how scaling decisions are made.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-registry/container-registry-skus) — the current tier table, limits and how to change tier.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Container Instances? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-instances/container-instances-overview) — container groups, Spot and confidential containers, NGroups and virtual nodes.

quiz.q: A vendor's price-import container runs for about ten minutes every night and then exits. Which service is the simplest fit, and which setting makes it stop billing when the work is done?
quiz.a: Azure Container Instances with the restart policy Never (a scheduled Container Apps job also works). ACI bills per second while the container group runs, so a ten-minute job costs ten minutes.

quiz.q: You deploy a container app with target port 80, but the image's web server listens on port 8080. What do you see, and how do you fix it?
quiz.a: The revision never becomes healthy and requests fail, because ingress forwards to a port where nothing listens. Set the ingress target port to 8080; the target port must match the port the process listens on.

quiz.q: Ibu Sari asks what the storefront container app costs at 03:00 when nobody is shopping. Its minimum is zero replicas. What do you tell her?
quiz.a: With no requests the revision scales to zero replicas, and on the Consumption plan zero replicas incur no compute charges. The trade-off is a cold start of a few seconds for the first shopper after the quiet spell.

quiz.q: Nusantara Retail wants its registry reachable only through a private endpoint and replicated to a second region. Which ACR tier does it need?
quiz.a: Premium. Private endpoints and geo-replication are Premium-only features; Basic and Standard offer neither.

quiz.q: Dewi switches the storefront to multiple revision mode and deploys v2. A minute later every shopper sees v2, not 20% of them. Why, and what should she do next time?
quiz.a: The traffic rule still sent 100% to the latest revision, and v2 became the latest. Pin 100% of traffic to v1 before deploying v2, test v2 on its own revision URL, then set the 80/20 split.

takeaways: A container image packages the app and its dependencies in immutable layers; build once, run the same image everywhere, and deploy explicit tags rather than latest.

Azure Container Registry is your private registry: Basic for learning, Standard for most production, Premium for geo-replication and private endpoints. Services pull with managed identities, and the admin user stays off.
Azure Container Instances runs a container group in seconds with per-second billing, but with no autoscaling or load balancing; it is ideal for jobs and quick tests.
Azure Container Apps adds environments, immutable revisions, HTTPS ingress, scale rules down to zero and traffic splitting, with no Kubernetes to manage. Get the target port right.
Pick the least platform that meets the need: Container Instances, then Container Apps, then AKS for the full Kubernetes API; App Service when it is simply a website.

lab.title: Package the storefront
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail wants one package for the storefront that runs the same everywhere, and a hosting option that costs nothing at three in the morning. You will create a private Azure Container Registry and import a small Microsoft sample web app into it as storefront:v1. You will run the same image in seconds on Azure Container Instances, then deploy it from your registry to Azure Container Apps, pulling with the app's managed identity instead of a password. Finally you will load-test it (replicas 0 → 5 → 0), release a second revision to 20% of requests, and repair a broken target port.

The sample image is a tiny Microsoft web app that listens on port 80 and shows the value of the TITLE environment variable as its page title. It was written for AKS walkthroughs, but that does not matter: a container image runs anywhere. Changing TITLE lets you see at a glance which copy or revision answered a request.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/13-containers-basic
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 13)
ACR_NAME="acrnusa${SUFFIX}"
APP=ca-nusa-storefront

- Make sure the resource providers this lab uses are registered. It is a one-time step per subscription and can take a minute or two:

for ns in Microsoft.ContainerRegistry Microsoft.ContainerInstance Microsoft.App Microsoft.OperationalInsights; do
  az provider register --namespace "$ns" --wait
done

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway. If Cloud Shell times out, open it again, cd back into this folder and re-run the source and variable lines above (and any LOGIN_SERVER=, FQDN= or REV1= lines from the task you were on).

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–5 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create a private registry and import the storefront image

A registry is the single source of truth for your images. az acr import copies an image from another registry inside Azure, so you do not need Docker in Cloud Shell.

ensure_rg "$RG" 13

az acr create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$ACR_NAME" \
  --sku Basic \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --output none

LOGIN_SERVER=$(az acr show --name "$ACR_NAME" --query loginServer --output tsv)
echo "Login server: $LOGIN_SERVER"

az acr import \
  --name "$ACR_NAME" \
  --source mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v1 \
  --image storefront:v1

az acr repository show-tags --name "$ACR_NAME" --repository storefront --output table
az acr show --name "$ACR_NAME" --query "{tier:sku.name, adminUser:adminUserEnabled}" --output table

Notice that the image now has a new name in your registry, storefront:v1, while its content (and digest) is identical to the Microsoft original. The admin user is false: nothing in this lab needs a registry password.

Optional — build in the cloud with ACR Tasks. The app/Dockerfile adds one layer on top of the sample image (a new default title). If your subscription allows ACR Tasks, build it in Azure:

az acr build --registry "$ACR_NAME" --image storefront:v1-built ./app

If you see TasksOperationsNotAllowed, your subscription uses Azure free credits and ACR Tasks runs are paused for it at the time of writing. Skip this step; the import above is all the lab needs.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Container registries › acrnusa… › Services › Repositories › storefront shows the tag and its digest. Settings › Access keys shows that the admin user is off.

Checkpoint: az acr repository show-tags lists v1, and the registry shows Basic with the admin user false.

Task 2 · Run a container in seconds with Container Instances

Container Instances runs one container group with no cluster and no VM to look after. You pay per second while it runs.

az container create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name ci-nusa-storefront \
  --image mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v1 \
  --os-type Linux \
  --cpu 1 --memory 1.5 \
  --ports 80 \
  --dns-name-label "nusa-store-${SUFFIX}" \
  --environment-variables TITLE="Nusantara Retail storefront on Container Instances" \
  --output none

az container show --resource-group "$RG" --name ci-nusa-storefront \
  --query "{state:instanceView.state, fqdn:ipAddress.fqdn}" --output table

ACI_FQDN=$(az container show --resource-group "$RG" --name ci-nusa-storefront --query ipAddress.fqdn --output tsv)
curl -s "http://${ACI_FQDN}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"
az container logs --resource-group "$RG" --name ci-nusa-storefront

Why does this container group pull from Microsoft's public registry and not from yours? To pull from a private registry, Container Instances needs a user-assigned managed identity that holds AcrPull; it cannot use a system-assigned identity for image pulls. Stretch goal 1 shows how. Container Apps, next, can use its own system-assigned identity. Notice also that the address is plain HTTP: Container Instances gives you an IP address and a DNS name, not a managed HTTPS endpoint.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Container instances › ci-nusa-storefront shows the state and FQDN on Overview, and Containers › Logs shows the same output as az container logs.

Checkpoint: the state is Running, the FQDN looks like nusa-store-<suffix>.<region>.azurecontainer.io, and curl prints <title>Nusantara Retail storefront on Container Instances</title>.

Task 3 · Deploy to Container Apps and pull with a managed identity

First create the environment, the secure boundary that your apps share. It takes two to four minutes. If you do not name a Log Analytics workspace, the CLI creates one for the environment's logs and tells you so.

az containerapp env create \
  --name cae-nusa \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --output none

Now create the app from your registry:

az containerapp create \
  --name "$APP" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --environment cae-nusa \
  --image "${LOGIN_SERVER}/storefront:v1" \
  --registry-server "$LOGIN_SERVER" \
  --registry-identity system \
  --ingress external \
  --target-port 80 \
  --min-replicas 0 \
  --max-replicas 5 \
  --scale-rule-name http-busy \
  --scale-rule-type http \
  --scale-rule-http-concurrency 10 \
  --env-vars TITLE="Nusantara Retail storefront v1" \
  --output none

What the important flags do:

Flag | Meaning
--registry-identity system | Turn on the app's system-assigned managed identity, grant it AcrPull on your registry and pull with it. Because the CLI does several steps for you, --no-wait is not allowed with this option.
--ingress external --target-port 80 | Publish the app on a public HTTPS address and forward requests to port 80, where the sample app listens.
--min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 5 | Scale to zero when idle; never run more than five replicas.
--scale-rule-type http --scale-rule-http-concurrency 10 | Add a replica for roughly every 10 concurrent requests.
--env-vars TITLE=... | A setting inside the revision template; changing it later creates a new revision.

Open the app and prove that no password was involved:

FQDN=$(az containerapp show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn --output tsv)
echo "https://${FQDN}"
curl -s "https://${FQDN}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"

az containerapp show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "properties.configuration.registries" --output table

PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az containerapp show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query identity.principalId --output tsv)
ACR_ID=$(az acr show --name "$ACR_NAME" --query id --output tsv)
az role assignment list --assignee "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --scope "$ACR_ID" --query "[].roleDefinitionName" --output tsv

The first request may take a few seconds: that is the cold start of the first replica.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open Container Apps › ca-nusa-storefront. Settings › Identity shows the system-assigned identity, Application › Containers shows the image from your registry, and Application › Revisions and replicas shows the running revision.

Checkpoint: curl prints <title>Nusantara Retail storefront v1</title>, the registries table shows your login server with identity system, and the role list prints AcrPull.

Task 4 · Watch it scale from zero to five and back

Check how many replicas are running now. Just after creation you may see 1; after about five quiet minutes you should see 0.

az containerapp replica list --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query "length(@)" --output tsv

Now play the 12.12 sale. The loop below sends about two minutes of traffic, 40 requests at a time, and counts the replicas every 15 seconds while it runs:

end=$((SECONDS + 120))
while (( SECONDS < end )); do
  seq 1 400 | xargs -P 40 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null "https://${FQDN}/"
done &
LOAD_PID=$!

for i in $(seq 1 8); do
  sleep 15
  echo "$(date +%T)  replicas: $(az containerapp replica list --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query 'length(@)' --output tsv)"
done
wait "$LOAD_PID"

The count climbs, and it never passes five because that is your maximum. When the load stops, the platform waits before it removes replicas: the cool-down before the last replica goes is 300 seconds by default. Check again after about seven minutes:

sleep 420
az containerapp replica list --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query "length(@)" --output tsv

Tip: Prefer the portal? ca-nusa-storefront › Monitoring › Metrics, metric Replica Count, aggregation Max, time range Last 30 minutes draws the whole 0 → 5 → 0 curve. The Requests metric shows the load you sent.

Checkpoint: you saw the replica count rise to 5 (and no higher) during the load, and fall back to 0 once traffic stopped.

Task 5 · Release v2 to 20% of shoppers

A canary release needs two active revisions and a traffic rule. The order of the steps matters.

# 1. Allow several revisions to be active at the same time.
az containerapp revision set-mode --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --mode multiple --output none

# 2. Pin all traffic to the current revision BEFORE you deploy anything new.
REV1=$(az containerapp show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query properties.latestRevisionName --output tsv)
az containerapp ingress traffic set --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --revision-weight "${REV1}=100" --output none

# 3. Deploy v2. A new environment variable is a revision-scope change, so it creates a new revision.
az containerapp update --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --set-env-vars TITLE="Nusantara Retail storefront v2" \
  --revision-suffix v2 \
  --output none
REV2="${APP}--v2"

# 4. Test v2 on its own address before any shopper sees it.
REV2_FQDN=$(az containerapp revision show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --revision "$REV2" \
  --query properties.fqdn --output tsv)
curl -s "https://${REV2_FQDN}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"

# 5. Canary: 80% stays on v1, 20% goes to v2.
az containerapp ingress traffic set --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --revision-weight "${REV1}=80" "${REV2}=20" --output none

az containerapp revision list --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{revision:name, active:properties.active, traffic:properties.trafficWeight, replicas:properties.replicas}" \
  --output table

Without step 2, the existing rule "100% to the latest revision" would have sent every shopper to v2 the moment it became ready. Now sample the public address 40 times and count which title answered:

for i in $(seq 1 40); do curl -s "https://${FQDN}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"; done | sort | uniq -c

Expect roughly 32 answers from v1 and 8 from v2; the exact numbers vary from run to run.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Application › Revisions and replicas (called Revision management in some portal versions) shows both revisions, their traffic percentages and their own URLs, and lets you change the split with a few clicks.

Checkpoint: the revision list shows two active revisions with traffic 80 and 20, and your sample shows both titles, mostly v1.

Break it and fix it

Rizky has decided that "all our apps listen on 8080 now" and updates the ingress without checking the image:

az containerapp ingress update --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --target-port 8080 --output none

for i in $(seq 1 5); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 30 "https://${FQDN}/"
done

Symptom: instead of 200 you get errors or timeouts (000 means curl gave up), and after a while the revisions report that they are not healthy:

az containerapp revision list --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{revision:name, health:properties.healthState, running:properties.runningState}" --output table

Notice that both revisions broke at once. Find the cause and repair it.

Hint

Compare az containerapp show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --query properties.configuration.ingress.targetPort with the port the sample app actually listens on (look back at --ports 80 in Task 2). Ingress is an application-scope setting: it applies to every revision at once and does not create a new revision.

Fix

az containerapp ingress update --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --target-port 80 --output none
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 60 "https://${FQDN}/"

The target port must match the port the process listens on inside the container. EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents it.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch13-<suffix> with everything in it: the registry, the container group, the Container Apps environment and app, and the Log Analytics workspace. Nothing in this lab lives outside the resource group: the AcrPull role assignment sits on the registry, and the app's system-assigned identity is deleted with the app. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
The registry DNS name acrnusa….azurecr.io is already in use | Registry names are global and someone else has yours | Choose another suffix: export SUFFIX=<5 new lowercase letters or digits> then source ../common/config.sh again and re-set the variables
(TasksOperationsNotAllowed) ACR Tasks requests for the registry … are not permitted | ACR Tasks runs are paused for subscriptions on Azure free credits | Skip the optional az acr build; az acr import is all the lab needs
(MissingSubscriptionRegistration) The subscription is not registered to use namespace 'Microsoft.App' | Resource provider not registered yet | Run the az provider register loop from Before you start and try again
DNS name label not available when creating the container group | Someone already uses that label in the region | Use another label, for example --dns-name-label "nusa-store-${SUFFIX}-2"
Container app creation fails with ... UNAUTHORIZED: authentication required ... | The identity's AcrPull assignment has not propagated yet, or your registry uses the ABAC permissions mode | Wait a minute and run az containerapp update --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --image "${LOGIN_SERVER}/storefront:v1". If az acr show --name "$ACR_NAME" --query roleAssignmentMode says AbacRepositoryPermissions, assign Container Registry Repository Reader to the app's identity instead of AcrPull
unrecognized arguments or the following arguments are required from an az containerapp command | An older Azure CLI (likely on a local PC) | Run az upgrade; if you use the Container Apps extension, az extension add --name containerapp --upgrade
The replica count never reaches 5 | Not enough concurrent requests | Raise the parallelism (-P 60) or the duration, and make sure FQDN is set
Replicas stay above 0 long after the test | The cool-down has not finished, or a load loop is still running | Wait 5–10 minutes; run jobs and kill %1 if a background loop is still alive
All 40 sample requests show v1 | v2 still has 0% of the traffic | az containerapp ingress traffic show --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" and repeat Task 5 step 5

1. Pull into Container Instances from your registry. Create a user-assigned identity, give it AcrPull, and let a second container group use it:

  sleep 60   # give the role assignment time to propagate

  az containerapp revision deactivate --name "$APP" --resource-group "$RG" --revision "$REV1"
